en: *Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Fascicle One, composed by Dharma Master Tanyan.

Now, I seek to investigate that the ultimate movement is boundless; its source cannot be known through ordinary thought or deliberation. It is profoundly penetrating and vast emptiness; it is beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
To reach this ultimate point and achieve such penetration—can it be anything other than the True Suchness (tathatā) of the mind?
If there is a substance that enables such profound penetration, the light of wisdom pervades the Dharma-realm; if one awakens to this supreme movement, the clouds of compassion fill all of space.

This is none other than Samantabhadra of wondrous virtue; he is the person capable of causing the clouds of compassion to fill the void. In meaning, this cannot be called "small," for it causes wisdom—
Its light pervades the entire dharma-realm. In meaning, it cannot be said not to be "Great. Because it cannot be said not to be Great, the name "Great" arises from this.
Because it is insufficient to call it "Small," the name "Small" vanishes from this. Therefore, this True Suchness is designated as "Great.
That which is traversed by compassion and wisdom is termed a "Vehicle. This concludes the general explanation.
Next is the detailed explanation. This specific meaning has three aspects. First is the meaning of the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*).

The essence of this mind, suchness (*tathatā*), universally constitutes the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Although all phenomena possess distinct characteristics such as arising and ceasing, or defilement and purity, this suchness is equal.
Because there is neither increase nor decrease. What is the meaning of this? If it were unable to serve as the substance for all phenomena universally, it might be called "small";
however, since it can indeed serve as the substance for all phenomena, it cannot be said not to be "great. Second is the meaning of the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahatva*).
This essence of *tathatā* has all virtues as its characteristic. What does this mean?
If this essence were deficient in any of these virtues, it might be called "small. Since it is fully endowed with immeasurable essential virtues, it cannot be said not to be "great.
Third is the meaning of the greatness of function: this characteristic of *tathatā* is able to give rise to both mundane and supramundane [phenomena].
It takes virtuous causes and effects as its function. How is this known?
If there were any cause and effect that did not arise from this, it might be called small; since all causes and effects arise from this, it cannot be said not to be great.
Because it is great in these three senses, compassion relies upon it to fill empty space, and wisdom rides upon it to pervade the dharma-realm. Great!
The name "Vehicle" (yāna) arises from this.
As for the expression "arousing faith," this Prajñā and Great Compassion do not arise without a cause; rather, faith is generated based on the Mahāyāna.
This is because those three types of sentient beings, being deluded and ignorant, do not understand these three kinds of great meanings within True Suchness (tathatā).
They do not give rise to faith or joy. Out of great compassion, the Bodhisattva composed this treatise so that they might develop right faith;
therefore, it is titled *Awakening of Faith*. Regarding the three types of sentient beings: first, there are those with the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Because of their ignorance, they give rise to various views of a self and do not believe that the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the nature of sentient beings. For the sake of causing them to have faith in their own bodies...

There is the meaning of the essential nature of *tathatā*. Furthermore, because it causes one to distance oneself from the faults of various views of a self, it demonstrates the meaning of the greatness of the essence of *tathatā*.
Second, because sentient beings who are inverted are obscured by darkness, they claim that the qualities of *tathatā* do not belong to them and thus fail to give rise to aspiration or seeking.
[The teaching] intends to cause them to believe that those qualities of *tathatā* can indeed be attained.

Furthermore, it causes those with the mind of a lame donkey—who lack the intent for progress—to distance themselves from such faults. It reveals the great meaning of the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness).

Third, regarding sentient beings with distracted minds due to emptiness: because they do not understand, they cling to non-existence as being "emptiness" and do not believe that *tathatā* possesses the inexhaustible meaning of being capable of producing merit.
To cause them to believe in these inexhaustible merits, [the teaching] further causes them to distance themselves [from their errors].
Because it delights in the transcendence of emptiness, it demonstrates the great significance of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding "discourse" (*śāstra*): if one wishes to cause these three types of sentient beings to give rise to right faith, it cannot be without a basis;
it must rely on discourse through questions and answers to reveal these three kinds of great significance. Only then will their faith become definitive; therefore, it is called "discourse."

Furthermore, this treatise is broadly divided into three parts from beginning to end: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination. The first three verses clarify the homage to the Triple Gem, the invocation of their power, and the request for their grace;
these constitute the Introduction. The section of the treatise beginning with "There is a Dharma" and following distinguishes the Main Body. At the end...
The final two verses clarify the propagation [of this work]. As for the necessity of paying homage:

since the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa himself was still situated on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣabhūmi*), if he had not received the empowerment of the Triple Gem, this profound and secret treasury could not have been proclaimed.

Therefore, homage must be paid. Once empowered by the sacred strength [of the Triple Gem], one is then able to speak. For this reason, the second [section] must present the discourse that ought to be delivered.
[The] Body. Why is it that the third [section], the Propagation, concerns only the Bodhisattvas’ original vows? It is because they seek only to benefit others and do not seek their own benefit.
The first section consists of two parts: the first two verses correctly clarify the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem, while the final verse clarifies the taking of refuge in the [Teacher].
The meaning of this is as follows: the first part is further divided into two sections. The initial two characters, "take refuge" (namas), correctly clarify the one who takes refuge;
the passage beginning with "throughout the ten directions" clarifies the object of veneration.

Regarding the expression "taking refuge," there are two intentions. First, it means to entrust one's own life of wisdom (prajñājīvita) to that which has been realized by oneself, desiring to preach based upon that realization.
Second, it means that through the majestic power of the Triple Gem, which can assist all who preach, the great sage Aśvaghoṣa surrendered his own life and requested their empowerment.

Regarding the objects of refuge, there is first a general statement followed by a specific one. The phrase "extending throughout the ten directions" is the general statement; "supreme" and what follows are the specific ones.
The initial mention of "extending throughout the ten directions" clarifies the scope of the refuge. The essence of refuge is twofold: first, the ten directions spoken of in terms of location;
second, the ten directions spoken of in terms of essence. The merits of the Triple Gem are like space, having no boundaries or limits.
To cause sentient beings to take refuge so that they may give rise to vast and inexhaustible merit, it is divided internally into three parts.
First, five phrases clarify the Buddha Jewel; next, one phrase clarifies the Dharma Jewel; and finally, one phrase clarifies the Sangha Jewel. Within the Buddha Jewel, there are three sections:
the first two phrases clarify the Dharmakāya Buddha; the third phrase clarifies the Sambhogakāya; and the final phrase clarifies the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Thus are the Three Jewels.
The meaning of this is explained extensively in another chapter. Regarding "the most supreme activity that is universally known," this clarifies the Buddha of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
How is this known? The treatise states: "All Bodhisattvas should perceive the Dharma-body as being constantly associated with the five activities, never departing from them even for a moment.

Therefore, we know that these five activities transcend the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*) and are thus called "most supreme. The five activities are: first, the activity of great compassion; second, the activity of correct... [text fragment ends]

The activities are: first, the activity of maturation; second, the activity of transformation; third, the activity of majestic power; fourth, the activity of skillful means; and fifth, the activity of the true teaching. These are fully detailed in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Regarding "pervasive knowledge," the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body universally illumines the dharma-realm; this refers to the two types of wisdom: the wisdom of principle (*pramāṇa*) and the wisdom of phenomena (*meya*).
Regarding "unimpeded mastery over form," this clarifies the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*): the sublime forms of all Buddhas have wisdom as their essence, because wisdom is sovereign.
"Form is also unimpeded. This "World-Savior of Great Compassion" clarifies the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), which follows sentient beings to extract them from suffering and bestow happiness;
thus it is called "Great Compassion. The passage beginning with "as well as that physical body and its marks" clarifies the *dharmakāya*. How is this known? The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:

"The form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the action-body (*karmakāya*) do not constitute the nature of the self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*) due to six causes. Since this [text] here speaks of "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), [it refers to the *dharmakāya*].

True Suchness (*tathatā*): one should know that this is primordially existent and not something that begins at a particular time. Because the preceding [section on] taking refuge has been explained in a comprehensive manner, it is mentioned here as well.
Now, when speaking of the characteristics of those two bodies, these refer to the nature of the two aforementioned bodies. First, regarding what was called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*):
This is a shift in terminology to indicate [the meaning]. It takes the *dharmadhātu* as its essential nature. "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) means non-differentiation and non-duality.
"Tao" (the ocean) signifies being profound, vast, and boundless; it neither increases nor decreases. Great-bodied sentient beings cannot fathom its bottom, hence it is called "profound.

This serves as a metaphor for the ocean of nature (*xinghai*), which is beyond the reach of those on the stages of learning. As for "vast," even the Bodhisattva of the Dharma-Cloud stage has not yet fully attained it.
This is the limit. Regarding "neither increasing nor decreasing": when the various streams pour into it, it does not increase; when it gives birth to all rivers, it does not decrease.

This is used as an analogy for the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*): wisdom is full and virtues are complete, yet it does not increase; delusions are eliminated and afflictions are stilled, yet it does not decrease.

"The treasury of immeasurable merit" clarifies that this treasury of the Dharma Jewel accumulates the merits of all practices throughout as many Ganges Rivers as there are, belonging to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because it is produced from this, it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. Regarding the phrase "one who practices according to reality," this sentence clarifies the Jewel of the Sangha.
All bodhisattvas constantly practice in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); therefore, they are called "those who practice according to reality."
Next, the meaning of the second homage is explained. Regarding these four intentions: "for the sake of sentient beings" refers first to clarifying the three types of sentient beings.
First, those with distracted minds regarding emptiness, who doubt that all things do not exist. Second, those who are non-Buddhists, who doubt the existence of a self among sentient beings.
Third, those of the two vehicles, who doubt the existence of a self among phenomena (*dharmātman*). [The purpose is] to eliminate their doubts.

Regarding "abandoning false attachments," this clarifies the second point: abandoning delusions and removing doubts. This refers to those prior to the [first] stage who, through their initial aspiration for joy, mistakenly grasp at emptiness and have confused minds;
they doubt that all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent, and thus do not believe that their own bodies possess the nature of *tathatā*.
To dispel these doubts, it is clarified that there exists the non-empty dharma of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, so as to cause them to depart from false attachments.
This section begins below to demonstrate the correct meaning. Regarding the treatment of those who harbor doubts as to whether [the ālayavijñāna] should be abandoned:

because those non-Buddhists, through their view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), conceive of a self within the body that acts as the agent and the experiencer, this doubt is dispelled by demonstrating that one's own body possesses the ālayavijñāna, which subsumes both the defiled and the pure, so that they may understand it.
Regarding the treatment of false views and the removal of attachment: by means of two...
The meaning of the *neyārtha* (provisional) teaching is that it takes suffering and impermanence as its ultimate tenet.

In order to reveal the four virtues of True Suchness—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and to cause [beings] to realize the intent of the teaching, practice accordingly, and ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood, these two [aspects] give rise to the antidotes for erroneous attachments below and arouse right faith in the Mahāyāna.
This third section clarifies the practices that are thus aroused, leading those three types [of beings].

Sentient beings, having given rise to correct faith in the three great meanings of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind, then initiate the "Section on the Practice of Faith" which describes the signs of the lower stage of analytical engagement with the path.
Regarding the phrase "so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed": this fourth point clarifies what is accomplished through practice.

Based on the aforementioned faith, upon reaching the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) and above, one attains the noble lineage (*ārya-gotra*), thereby ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. This is as follows:

This begins the section on the benefits of exhorting others to practice. Therefore, the treatise below states: "If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to cowardice, one should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas."
In the second section of the prose commentary, the actual body of the treatise is formally presented. This section contains three parts: first, a brief clarification of the introductory context;

next, the establishment of the chapter headings following the statement "there are five divisions"; and finally, the detailed explanation of each chapter according to its respective headings, beginning with the section on causes and conditions.
"Existence of the Dharma" refers to the true substance of the single mind, the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*).

It is that which enables one to give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna and causes sentient beings to rely upon it for practice, thereby increasing their pure faith. Therefore, it "should be explained": Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time all rely on this Dharma to achieve pure faith.
Consequently, the Master of the Treatise, following the constant principle of the source, has set forth and revealed it for those who have not yet [realized it].
Having heard that the discourse consists of five divisions, the following section clarifies the second part: the opening of the chapters. This contains three internal sections.

First, the initial chapter clarifies the opening of the introductory division (*nidāna*). Next, the subsequent three chapters clarify the opening of the main body (*samyak-śāsana*). Finally, one chapter opens the section on the dissemination (*parīndanā*). Thus it begins.
Since there is a reason for this exposition, I have first clarified its sequence. Once the meaning of the sequence is manifest, the primary doctrine (saddharma) is proclaimed.

Therefore, secondly, I shall distinguish the primary doctrine. Since the foundation of the doctrine has been established, thirdly, I shall praise the excellence of this treatise so as to transmit its benefits to the future.

The section on explanation is further divided into three parts. First is the explanation of the introductory section (*nidāna*). Second, from the "Establishment of the Meaning" (*siddhānta*) onwards, the main body (*śarīra*) is analyzed.
Finally, from the "Exhortation to Practice and Benefits" (*anuśaṃsā*) onwards, the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*) is explained.
The introduction (*nidāna*) is further divided into three parts. First, the section on the causal conditions (*nidāna-vibhāga*) introduces the title and the commencement of the discourse.

Second, from the question "It is asked" onwards, the causes and conditions for the commencement of the discourse are explained. Third, from the question "It is asked regarding the *sūtra*" onwards, the dialogue between question and answer follows.
This clarifies the purpose for which it must be explained.

Within the second section, concerning the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. The answer consists of three sections: first, a general response citing the teachings;
second, a detailed explanation of the eight kinds of causes and conditions, beginning with "How so..."; third, [the conclusion] beginning with "Since this is so... and so forth.
Third, the response to the question.
As for what constitutes the eight [topics], this is introduced by way of a preliminary inquiry.
From the first item below, the chapters and sections are explained. Within these eight, the first is general, while the latter seven are specific.
It is distinct. Regarding the general characteristics of causes and conditions, there are two intended meanings.

First, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss; that is, to cause them to leave behind the sufferings of *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) death, and to attain the unsurpassed Nirvana characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This clarifies the distinction from the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Second, "not seeking worldly fame, profit, appearances, or respect" clarifies...
Unlike ordinary beings who merely seek worldly benefits and engage in conventional discourse, [the Buddha] speaks in order to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata and so forth.
From this point forward, the specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) are explained. This section consists of three parts: the first three [verses] provide the introductory context;
the next two cause all sentient beings to correctly penetrate the profound fundamental meaning, rather than mistaking the coarse and shallow principles of the Hīnayāna for the ultimate truth.

[The preceding section] concludes. This [section] then initiates the following to demonstrate the correct meaning (*samyak-artha*). It is for the sake of causing sentient beings with roots of goodness to achieve accomplishment and reach the stage of non-retrogressive faith;

it is for the sake of causing those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), and for those bodhisattvas at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) to enter the assembly of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and become capable of non-retrogression.

This [section] then initiates the following to distinguish the characteristics of setting out upon the path (*pratipatti-mārga-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*). It is for the sake of [causing] those with very slight roots of goodness...
Regarding "the arising": for the sake of those sentient beings with the view of a self who have newly entered the Buddha-dharma, this shows the conceptualization of practicing faith;

this initiates the subsequent section on "Practicing Faith. For the sake of showing the expedient means to eliminate the karmic obstacles of evil, it is addressed to those *icchantikas* who have newly given rise to faith, stating that they shall eliminate the karmic obstacles of the net of false views. This passage has two parts; the first sentence is as follows:
It eliminates karmic obstacles. By skillfully guarding the mind so that afflictions do not arise, one immediately leaves behind the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This gives rise to the antidote for the erroneous attachments mentioned below, which will also be explained extensively later.

Regarding the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as antidotes for the mental faults of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles: *śamatha* is the realization of *tathatā*, while *vipaśyanā* is the thorough understanding [of phenomena].

Regarding the wisdom of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-jñāna*): how does it serve as an antidote? Since all phenomena are identical to suchness (*tathatā*), it prevents ordinary beings from dwelling in attachment to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) within the world.
Having realized that there is no suffering to be feared, it remedies the timid views of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Through the wisdom of the understanding of causes and conditions, one knows that the two causes of good and evil bring about the two retributions of suffering and pleasure; having heard this, ordinary beings abandon evil and cultivate goodness.

This remedies the fault of failing to cultivate the roots of goodness. Upon hearing that karma and its fruits are never lost, those of the Two Vehicles give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and take pity on suffering sentient beings;
this remedies the fault of failing to give rise to great compassion. This constitutes the application of the lower stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote.

As for "single-mindedly recollecting the skillful means to be born before the Buddha and giving rise to non-retrogressive faith," this indicates the aspiration of an outer-worldling (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), intended to prevent them from falling back.

This is the introduction to the following section. Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds may become timid and weak, fearing they will regress.
Therefore, they are taught to focus their mindfulness on the aspiration to be born in the Pure Land so that they do not lose their faith;
this is done to demonstrate the benefits and to encourage them in practice. First, when sentient beings practice according to the Dharma, they obtain these benefits. This is the introduction.
The following is the section on exhorting others to practice for their benefit.
The reasons for composing this treatise based on such causes and conditions constitute the third summary of the benefits.
From the question "It has already been stated... onwards, the third major section clarifies the purpose for which it must be taught. This text consists of two parts; the first...
The question is followed by the answer. The answer contains three parts. First is the general response: because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, it is necessary to teach.
Second is the specific response, beginning with "As the Tathāgata was in the world... Third is the concluding summary, beginning with "Thus, this treatise..."
Regarding the statement that the activities of the mental faculty (*manas*) are unequal: those of sharp faculties delight in brevity, while those of dull faculties prefer extensiveness.
Some attain understanding directly from the sūtras, while others only realize it through the treatises.
Regarding "The Tathāgata being in the world," there are two parts within the subsequent detailed explanation of the characteristics. First, it clarifies that there is no need for teaching.
Following "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa," it clarifies that there is a need for teaching. Within the section on not needing to teach, there are five points.

"The Tathāgata being in the world" refers to the excellence of the first period. "Sentient beings have sharp faculties" clarifies the excellence of the second: those who receive the Dharma and are able to explain it.
From "human" downwards: the third clarifies the excellence of the speaker; the single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by each species.

This clarifies the fourth [excellence]: the superiority of the benefit of the Dharma teaching. This clarifies the Tathāgata’s three wheels of conversion: the body manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); [the speech is the wheel of Dharma; and the mind is the wheel of wisdom].
The radiance of light dispels obscurations; the mouth employs sound to expound the Dharma; and the mind applies inner wisdom to those who hear it.

Thus, there is no need for formal treatises. This fifth point concludes that they are unnecessary. Since the vessels of the Dharma are already refined and the times are not those of the Semblance Age, having encountered the powerful conditions of meeting a Buddha, the perfect voice benefits all universally.
Whatever doubts exist are dispelled, like beholding a reflection in a mirror; therefore, there is no need for treatises. If...

After my parinirvāṇa, there will be two types [of practitioners]. The first are those who attain understanding by relying on the sūtras; the second are those who achieve awakening by means of the śāstras.

Regarding those who attain understanding by relying on the sūtras, there are again two types. The first are those of dull faculties, who must rely on extensive textual elaborations before they can finally attain understanding.
Second are those of sharp faculties, who, by means of their physical and mental vigor, can attain much realization from hearing little;
these two types of persons do not require further discussion. There may also be sentient beings who attain understanding through reliance on treatises (*śāstra*);

these likewise are of two kinds: first, those who attain understanding after relying on extensive treatises; second, those who attain awakening by means of concise ones. Regarding these latter two types of persons, one must [proceed as follows]:

Regarding the exposition of the treatise: this demonstrates the distinctions among the conditions for receiving and understanding it. That one should hear extensively while practicing concisely demonstrates that the faculties and practices are not equal.

Such a treatise is intended to comprehensively encompass [all teachings], up to the point where it should be said that "this treatise must be explained. This is the third summary of the intent for which it must be taught.
Within this, the vast, profound Dharma and its boundless meanings are subsumed within the single mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It has no exterior; therefore, it is called "vast. This very essence of mind is what is termed the "profound Dharma" because it is devoid of the two kinds of self.
It is not encompassed by the three periods of time; therefore, it is said to be "boundless."

Next is the section on establishing the doctrine (*shèyìfēn*). Following the first part of the text, the second part now explains the main body of the treatise (*zhèngzōng*), interpreting the three preceding chapters in sequence;

this constitutes three sub-sections. First, the establishment of the doctrine is explained; second, the explanation of the doctrine is explained; and third, the "Section on Cultivating Faith" (*xiūxìn xīnfēn*) is explained.

Regarding the first of these, there are two parts: first, concluding the previous section and introducing the current one; second, from "Mahāyāna" onwards, the actual establishment of the doctrine is clarified. This section contains three parts.
First, the citation of the teaching to set forth its meaning. Second, from “What are the two? onwards, the enumeration of names by number.
Third, from “That which is called ‘dharma’” onwards, the explanation according to those names.
Regarding the term *mahāyāna*, it is translated here as "Great Vehicle" (*dàchéng*). This phrase provides a general indication of the essential tenets of this entire treatise;
it takes the Great Vehicle as its primary doctrine.

Within the explanation based on the name, there are two parts. First is the explanation of the establishment of the doctrine, which serves as the basis for what follows in the section "Manifesting the Correct Meaning. It relies upon...
From "The dharma of single-mindedness" down to "because of the arising of activity and perfuming, there is no interruption" is the second explanation establishing the thesis.
That is, from "Next, regarding the self-substance and characteristics of True Suchness" down to "because of the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness."
The explanation of the establishment of the Dharma-gates has two parts. Regarding the term "Dharma," this refers to the title of the chapter.

The section beginning with "that which is called the mind of sentient beings" contains three internal divisions. First, the phrase "the mind of sentient beings" generally presents the essence of the Dharma;

this gives rise to the subsequent statement: "Based on the single mind, there are two gates of Dharma. The phrase "this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas" is the second [division].
This clarifies the meaning of the application of the mind-dharma (*cittadharma*). That is to say, the two gates that follow below each comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
This explains how the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpādanirodha*) each encompass all dharmas.

From "Based on this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed" onwards is the third explanation; it clarifies that this mind encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas. That is to say, it gives rise to the following.
The section beginning with "The mind as suchness" (citta-tathatā) provides a specific explanation of the two gates of suchness and birth-and-death.
First, the term "the mind of sentient beings" (sattva-citta) generally indicates the substance of phenomena; that is, the minds of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Because they are able to manifest [phenomena], they are called "dharmas. The phrase "this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas" is the second point, clarifying the nature of the mind-dharma.

Regarding the functional application of meaning: this mind is twofold. First, it is the capacity for discrimination, which relies on the characteristics of names and words to manifest the meaning of phenomenal forms;
this encompasses worldly dharmas. Second, it is the essence of discrimination, namely the characteristic of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind, which can demonstrate the supramundane meaning;
this encompasses supramundane dharmas. To manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna based upon this mind is as follows:
The third section clarifies the meaning by relying on the Dharma. This passage consists of two parts: first, the general statement; second, the explanation beginning with "Why is this so?

To clarify the meaning of the Mahāyāna by relying on this general statement is because this mental dharma possesses three kinds of meaning, and it is for this reason that it can demonstrate the meaning of the Great Vehicle.
The intent of the question "Why is this so? is as follows: the mind of sentient beings is a worldly phenomenon (*saṃsārika-dharma*).
It should only encompass worldly dharmas; why, then, can it also encompass supramundane dharmas? The passage beginning with "This mind has the characteristic of true suchness" provides the answer.
Because this mind possesses three characteristics: first, the characteristic of the mind’s true suchness, which can reveal the essence of the Mahāyāna and thus encompasses supramundane dharmas;
second, the characteristic of the mind’s arising and ceasing, which can reveal the self-nature, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna, and thus...

This section on "Encompassing the Worldly Dharmas" consists of two parts. First, the statement "this is the aspect of the mind as suchness" (tathatā-lakṣaṇa) introduces the subsequent detailed explanation of the gate of the mind as suchness.

Second, the passage beginning with "this is the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind" introduces the subsequent detailed explanation of the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Regarding "this is the aspect of the mind as suchness": the essence of the mind is real; this is precisely suchness.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it can manifest the essence of the Mahāyāna": True Suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely the essential body of the Mahāyāna dharma.

Regarding the phrase "it is the causal condition for the arising and ceasing of the mind," there are two parts to this passage. First, the statement "it is the characteristic of the causal condition for the arising and ceasing of the mind" gives rise to the subsequent chapter on the arising and ceasing of the mind.
The phrase "because it can demonstrate the essence, body, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna" gives rise to... [the subsequent section].
Below, because there is the meaning of the perfuming of four kinds of dharmas, there is the section on the uninterrupted arising of defiled and pure dharmas. The initial text has three parts.
"The mind's arising and ceasing" refers to the two characters "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) in the section explaining the arising and ceasing of the mind.

The second part refers to the section explaining the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of dharmas, beginning with the words "Furthermore, the causes and conditions for the arising of dharmas. Regarding their characteristics—
One word. Third, the section beginning with "Next, to further distinguish the characteristics of arising and ceasing" is the Chapter Explaining the Characteristics.

Regarding the statement that this refers to the "characteristics of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind": when the momentum of the mind first begins to arise, it is termed "arising"; because the momentum of the mind is exhausted, it is termed "ceasing.
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) transforms and becomes the mental factors of merit; the fundamental consciousness transforms and becomes the sense objects (*viṣaya*).

The object serves as the condition for the arising of the mind. Due to these causes and conditions, all defiled phenomena flow continuously without interruption from beginningless time, while all pure phenomena increase in succession.
As for the characteristic, it refers to the coarse and subtle characteristics of the mind that has arisen.
Regarding the phrase "because it can demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna": this means that the Mahāyāna possesses its own essence, characteristics, and function;
it does not mean that the mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) of arising and ceasing possess an essence that establishes these characteristics and functions.

Furthermore, although these characteristics of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses—the mental phenomena of arising and ceasing—differ infinitely from moment to moment throughout their succession, [they are traced] to the ultimate...

The substantial reality has no further distinct characteristics; therefore, it is called the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness). This very characteristic is used to demonstrate the essence of the Mahāyāna.

How is it demonstrated? Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the seed of all consciousnesses, if this seed-consciousness were of a different substance [from them], [the Mahāyāna essence could not be shown].

The various consciousnesses that arise [from it] were previously considered to have distinct individual entities. However, upon investigating these consciousnesses, because they lack individual entities, it is verified that the essence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is non-dual.
This clarifies the first point: demonstrating its essential nature. Second, regarding the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the mind:

this clarifies that this fundamental consciousness is the seed of the consciousnesses of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Furthermore, when these seeds have not yet arisen, they are with that fundamental [consciousness].
The consciousnesses rely upon one another and conceal one another, such that their own natures are not manifest. When they arise, their functional capacities then appear;

therefore, they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing, which can demonstrate the characteristics of the Mahāyāna. As for what is called "manifesting function," it is because the merits of this consciousness are accomplished through mutual support before and after;

this verifies that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has the nature of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, at the time of its causality, the storehouse consciousness possesses the karmic functions of aversion and seeking.

At the time of fruition, it gives rise to responsive transformations to benefit sentient beings; this demonstrates the meaning of the Mahāyāna’s function (*vṛtti*). Why are the self-nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*) of the Mahāyāna spoken of?
If one relies on the Mahāyāna, the uninterrupted perfuming of defilement and purity is clarified, whereas in the Hīnayāna it does not exist.
Therefore, the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind can demonstrate the self-nature, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning": from here below begins the second chapter, the Exposition of the Meaning. This serves as the introduction to the subsequent chapter, the Exposition of the Correct Meaning.

Furthermore, the section beginning with "Next, as for the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness" constitutes the second part, the Exposition of the Establishment of the Meaning. This text has three sections.
First, the statement "As for 'meaning,' there are three kinds" indicates the number of items presented in this chapter. As for the phrase "What are they," and so forth...
The second question concerns the enumeration. Regarding the phrase "the first is as follows" (*yī xià zhī yī zhě yǐ xià*), this indicates the separate explanations of the chapters.

This essence, characteristics, and function give rise to the following two chapters. First, regarding the two sections on essence and characteristics, the text states: "Next, concerning the essence and characteristics of True Suchness" (*fùcì zhēnrú zì tǐxiàng zhě*), which serves as a dual heading for these two chapters to extensively explain their meaning.
Third, regarding the section on function, the text states: "Next, concerning the function of True Suchness" (*fùcì zhēnrú yòng zhě yǐ*).
The following is the detailed explanation of the Chapter on Function (*vṛtti*).
Regarding what is called "the greatness of essence" (*svabhāva-mahattva*), this establishes the meaning of the greatness of the essence of *tathatā*.

The passage beginning with "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*) explains that all phenomena are equal in *tathatā*, neither increasing nor decreasing. "All" refers to the defiled and pure [phenomena] and so forth; it brings to rest the singularity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. It is "such" because it is not destroyed in the mundane world and is not exhausted in the supramundane world; because all phenomena are neither different nor dual, they are such.
The true suchness of the one mind is the essence of all phenomena—both common and uncommon—and is termed "equality.
Regarding its being without increase or decrease: when defiled phenomena of affliction manifest, they appear based upon the substance of the mind, yet they possess no inherent self-nature.
It may increase. The substance of the mind is capable of manifestation, yet this illuminating nature and its merit do not perish.
It is like a mirror and its images: when a defiled image appears, there is no substance in the mirror that increases; the functional power of the pure mirror’s illuminating nature does not diminish.

If afflictions were to appear with a substantial body that could increase, then upon their cessation, one could observe a corresponding decrease. Since they do not increase while manifesting, there is nothing to decrease when they pass away.

This clarifies that, regarding the nature of phenomena as characterized by conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that can be distinguished in terms of increase or decrease.

Although the essence of dependent cognition (*paratantra-vijñāna*) serves as the basis for both defilement and purity, its essence is devoid of mentation; therefore, while in bondage it is not originally defiled, and upon emerging [from bondage] it is not newly purified.
Being unchanging from beginning to end, one cannot distinguish increase or decrease with respect to it. As this treatise states: "All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas..."

One awakens to the fact that all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are without increase or decrease; they are not born in the past limit (pūrvānta) nor do they perish in the future limit (aparānta). Thus, the treatise explains this extensively. Regarding the "Greatness of Characteristics" (lakṣaṇamahatva):
this is the second [section], which establishes the meaning of the Greatness of the Characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā). That is to say, regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, there are two meanings.

First, the meaning of "encompassing" (*saṃgraha*); second, the meaning of "arising" (*utpatti*). Because it is sustained by the True Suchness (*tathatā*) through the absence of biased habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time rely upon this arising;
thus, it receives this name. Regarding "possessing the qualities of uncontaminated nature" (*anāsrava-dharmatā-guṇa-samanvāgata*):
this True Suchness not only sustains uncontaminated habitual tendencies, but its essence also possesses the capacity to encompass qualities exceeding the number of sands in the Ganges. As it is said:
The *Treatise* below states: "Because its own essence possesses the meaning of being fully endowed with pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges and so forth, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is also called the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. This constitutes the 'Greatness of Characteristics' (*lakṣaṇamahattva*).

Previously, the 'Greatness of Essence' (*svabhāvamahattva*) was clarified, demonstrating that this originally enlightened mind-nature universally serves as the essence for both ordinary beings and sages, as well as for the defiled and the pure; there is not a single dharma that exists outside of this mind."
Therefore, it attains the name "Great. Now, regarding what is called the "greatness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamahatva*):

this refers to the aforementioned essence of mind (*cittatattva*), which is not merely pervasive and profoundly pure in its substance, but is also capable of inherently possessing merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges. By means of these very merits, the greatness of characteristics is manifested.

Regarding "the greatness of function": the third section establishes the meaning of the greatness of the function of *tathatā* (suchness). This corresponds to the passage beginning with "Next, as for the function of *tathatā*" and below, which constitutes the chapter explaining the function of *tathatā*.

While the preceding explanation of essence and characteristics applies to both the hidden and the manifest states, this explanation of the greatness of function relies solely upon the state of being free from entanglements (*niṣkleśa*).

This does not mean that during the time of being in defilement (*saṃkleśa*), there is no functional activity of seeking liberation through aversion [to suffering]; rather, it is simply that the application of effort was not yet complete. Now, having reached...

At the time of fruition, when the causal practices have reached their ultimate fulfillment, the fundamental Dharma-body manifests through the arising of response and transformation bodies to benefit sentient beings, continuing without interruption throughout the limits of the future.

Since these manifestations exhaust the entire Dharma-realm, there is no goodness that is not produced; it is by means of this very activity that the great significance of its function is demonstrated.
This passage consists of two parts. First, regarding that which can produce mundane and supramundane goodness, it arises from within the True Suchness itself.
However, from "Nevertheless, there is the inconceivable karma" onwards is the second section on the functional activity of the two Buddhas regarding retribution.
From "Because this is what all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted" onwards is the second [sub-section], which generates the internal application of True Suchness;
it is the text concerning how all Tathāgatas, while originally in the causal stage, gave rise to great compassion, cultivated the various *pāramitās*, and gathered and transformed sentient beings.
Regarding the initial statement that [the Buddha] can produce all mundane and supramundane causes and fruits of goodness:

this refers to the two types of Buddhas—the *vipāka* (retribution) Buddha and the *nirmāṇa* (response) Buddha—who benefit sentient beings according to their capacities. If we speak in terms of the response Buddha, he teaches all sentient beings the roots of goodness pertaining to humans and devas; these are termed "mundane goodness."

If one generates the untainted (anāsrava) mind of the Mahāyāna, it is called supramundane goodness (*lokottara-kuśala*). If, based on the fruit of the Reward-Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) and the ten kings born of the various Bodhisattvas, it is called mundane goodness (*laukika-kuśala*).
That which remains in constant nirvāṇa until the end of the future is called supramundane goodness.

This second [section] clarifies that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not only named as such because it possesses the aforementioned three meanings, but is also the vehicle upon which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden.
It is great; furthermore, it serves as the vehicle for all great beings. It demonstrates the vastness of this True Suchness (tathatā) upon which all bodhisattvas ride.
There are none among those who practice who do not rely upon it, for by means of it they travel to the stage of the Tathāgata.
This great significance is revealed not merely because it is a vehicle for many people, but because those who ride this vehicle reach [the ultimate goal].
"Great place" further manifests greatness. This is the manifestation of greatness by means of the vehicle (*yāna*). Therefore, the treatise below states:

"When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were originally on the stage of the causal ground, they gave rise to great compassion and cultivated the various *pāramitās*, until they realized that all sentient beings and their own bodies are equal in *tathatā* (suchness), and because they perceived the original *dharmakāya*, the six *pāramitās* were thereby perceived."

The contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Innate enlightenment devoid of conceptualization (*anupalambha*) is the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*). The Bodhisattva, relying upon these two causes—the contributory and the direct—reaches the fruit of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is said that they "arrive at the stage of the Tathāgata."

The section on establishing the thesis has already been explained. Next is the section on the detailed explanation. From here below begins the second part, the section on the detailed explanation, within the main text of the orthodox teaching.

This section contains four parts. First is the transition from the preceding to the subsequent. Regarding the phrase "there are three kinds of explanation," this is the second part, which introduces the chapter and states the number.
The phrase "What are the three? is the third part, which enumerates the names. The phrase "to reveal the correct meaning" is the fourth part.
The detailed explanation follows the names. The internal explanation proceeds by distinguishing the sequence of the first three chapters.

Within the explanation of the first chapter, there are two parts: first, the citation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the meaning based on the passage beginning with "Based on the one mind. Within this latter explanation, there are three sections.
First, the detailed explanation of the "Section on Establishing the Doctrinal Gates" within the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" above.

Next, from "Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the essence of True Suchness" onwards, is the second part, the explanation of the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" within the "Section on Explaining the Five Meanings" above.

Next, from "Next, demonstrating [the gate] arising from the gate of birth-and-death" onwards, is the third part, which correctly clarifies the skillful means for entering the dharma-meaning of True Suchness through contemplative practice. This concludes the explanation of the first passage.
There are four [sections]. Regarding the statement, "Based on the single dharma of the one mind, there are two kinds of gates":

this first [section] cites the number by way of the dharma. "What are the two?"—this second [section] lists the names. "These two meanings establish the aforementioned 'establishment of the gates of dharma';

as for what is called 'dharma,' it refers to the mind of sentient beings"—this third [section] provides a brief explanation of the two gates, encompassing the meaning of the dharma. What is the meaning of this?
What is meant by this? To establish this meaning: if there were a distinction between these two gates, then there would have to be inclusion and non-inclusion for them to be called distinct.
Since they are already subsumed as a whole, how can their differing characteristics be clarified?

By stating that these two gates are not mutually exclusive, it is shown that the distinction between the two gates is not asserted on the basis of a difference in substance through inclusion or non-inclusion; rather, it reveals this [point].

Only through the mutual perfuming of these two gates does the sense of "encompassment" arise. If the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind encompasses all defiled phenomena, it must take True Suchness as its substance;
only then can it sustain the gate of the True Suchness of the mind.

As for the gate that encompasses all pure phenomena, even though it is by means of the deluded mind that one is able to know their names and meanings, it is only through repeated perfuming that one begins with pure phenomena; this constitutes the function of sustaining and encompassing.
The basis has no substantial reality. If one is separated from mental conceptualization, then all appearances of objective realms are verified to lack substantial reality.

How is this verified? If these various phenomena each possessed a distinct intrinsic nature, then those who have transcended conceptualization would be experiencing a distortion, while those who have not transcended conceptualization would perceive things as they truly are.
However, all noble beings (āryas) have transcended deluded thought, and yet—
Since it is not inverted, it is verified that form and the other aggregates lack substantial reality.

Therefore, from the phrase "all dharmas" onwards, the third section establishes the name of *tathatā* (suchness) through seven kinds of meanings. "Therefore" refers to the preceding three kinds of meanings.

"All dharmas" refers to those subsumed within *tathatā*, namely the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. "From the very beginning, they are free from the characteristics of verbal expression" reveals [this].
This suchness is the antidote to verbal expression; therefore, it renders verbal expression devoid of corresponding meaning. Regarding "being free from the marks of names":
if even verbal expression does not correspond [to it], how could these names serve as its cause? Regarding "being free from the marks of mental objects":
this reveals that suchness is not the sphere of discursive thought (vitarka) or investigation (vicāra). Regarding "ultimate equality": this demonstrates that suchness...
It is like space, which neither increases nor decreases, and possesses no change or alteration.

While all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) undergo transformation from beginning to end, this *tathatā* (suchness) remains forever unchanging and indestructible; it demonstrates the ultimate truth and ultimate reality.
"Only this one mind" refers to the fact that the aforementioned dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have no separate individual essences; they are only this one mind.
"Therefore it is named True Suchness" (tathatā) clarifies the meaning by providing the name.

"All verbal designations are provisional names without reality, even to the point of being unobtainable" means that this fourth section explains how all delusive dharmas have names but lack reality, existing only in accordance with deluded thoughts and being ultimately unattainable.

Regarding "attainable": this demonstrates that all names and verbal expressions are merely the products of the conceptualization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and that nothing real can be attained therein.
As for the term "Tathatā" (Suchness): from here below begins the fifth section, which eliminates secret doubts. The doubt consists in saying that the aforementioned Tathatā is devoid of...
All verbal expressions—even this name "Suchness" (tathatā)—are themselves verbal expressions. How could other words exist while being entirely free from this name "Suchness"?
If one does not depart from the name "Suchness," then Suchness itself would possess the characteristic of verbal expression.
The previous argument is thus refuted. From here on, the doubts are severed.
As for the statement that "even *tathatā* (suchness) has no characteristics": all names are established based upon various differentiated characteristics;
since this *tathatā* is not characterized by existence, how could any verbal expression possibly name it? This refers to verbal expression...
As for the ultimate limit, all verbal expressions have already been transcended and exhausted; only the name "True Suchness" (tathatā) remains.
Beyond this point, there is no further name. Regarding "using words to dispel words": it means using these words for True Suchness to dispel all other words.
How are they dispelled? By being free from names and words, it is called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). Because it is "true," false names are dispelled;
because it is "such," divergent names are dispelled. This essence of True Suchness has nothing that can be dispelled.

To show that defilements and burdens are entirely exhausted such that even "dispelling" does not apply—because all phenomena are entirely true—this establishes the preceding meaning that there is nothing to be dispelled. If phenomena were not true, [they could be dispelled].
One must employ antidotes to dispel them; yet because all are truly such, there is nothing further to be dispelled. Nor is there anything that can be established.
Generally speaking, what is called "establishment" refers to a case where no intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) exists originally, and one first intends to posit it—this may be termed "establishment.

But this is simply the way things are (*dharmatā*); therefore, there is nothing that can be established. Because all phenomena are identical to suchness (*tathatā*), the preceding point—that there is nothing to be established—is proven. If a phenomenon...
If it were not thus, there would be something that could be established; because it is identical with Thusness (tathatā), there is nothing that can be established.

One should know that the statement that "all phenomena are ineffable" is intended to encourage students to seek the Truth through words; that they are "inconceivable" indicates that one should seek Thusness by extinguishing discursive thought.
Therefore, the name "True Thusness" (bhūta-tathatā) reveals that this Thusness is neither a dharma that can be spoken nor a dharma that can be conceived. Hence, [it is not...]
One may employ speech and thought to seek this name and its meaning.
Next, the second question and answer is explained to clarify contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This passage has two parts: first the question, then the answer. The question asks:
"If such is the meaning," which refers back to the previously stated principle that it is neither expressible nor conceivable. Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings," it means:
Regarding the person who cultivates the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*): how can they accord with it and thereby gain entry?
Since this True Suchness is ineffable and inconceivable, yet those who cultivate contemplation all possess speech and thought, one might think that practitioners would be unable to enter it.
Next, the response is revealed: the answer says, "If one knows all phenomena"—that is, phenomena which are the manifestations of one's own mind.

Although it is said that there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken, this is shown because there is no speaker due to the absence of self, and there is nothing to be spoken because of the absence of external objects.
To say that there is neither the capacity to speak nor the object of thought is likewise so. This is called "conforming.

If there were a difference between the speaker and that which is spoken, one would be riding upon the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). Since there is no difference between the speaker and that which is spoken, it is called "conforming to suchness."
Furthermore, as for "being free from thought," it was originally thought that there were dharmas existing apart from the mind, which one would then grasp through thought.

Since there are no dharmas outside the mind, one instead perceives one's own mind; what need is there then for thought? By reflecting in this way, thought naturally subsides of its own accord, and thus it is called "freedom from thought."

One is called an "attainer of entry" because they have turned back from their original state after wandering outward. Coming from a beginningless past, they realize that the objects of perception are non-existent;
by ceasing their mental activity and returning to the source, they are said to have "entered."

Next, the second [section], the characteristic of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-lakṣaṇa*), is explained. This passage contains three parts. First, "Furthermore, regarding *tathatā*, based on verbal expression and conceptual differentiation, there are two kinds of meanings":
this first part enumerates the categories with respect to the phenomena (*dharma*). Second, "What are the two? and so forth: this sequentially lists the names and provides distinct explanations.
Third, "That which is called 'emptiness' (*śūnyatā*)," and so forth: this is the extensive explanation based on the names.
Regarding the term "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*): this is the initial enumeration of its names. It clarifies that the substance of this true *tathatā* (suchness) is in fact empty;

it is not an emptiness that is merely nominal. As for the phrase "because it can ultimately manifest the reality": this emptiness is not called "empty" merely because it is free from all delusive phenomena;
furthermore, because it can manifest the true existence of the immeasurable merits of *tathatā*, it is termed "emptiness as it truly is. As [it is said]:
Because one perceives that the second moon is empty, one is able to demonstrate that the true moon is not empty.
That which is "not empty according to reality" is the second name listed here; it clarifies that this *tathatā* (suchness) is indeed not empty.

This "non-emptiness" has two meanings: first, it is called non-empty because it possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmas*).
This second section clarifies that it is further endowed with merit, and thus is said to be "not empty.
Regarding what is called "emptiness," the third section below provides a detailed explanation based on its names. First, the meaning of emptiness is explained; next, non-emptiness is explained.

Within the explanation of emptiness, there are three parts: first, a general explanation of the chapter title; second, a specific refutation [of misconceptions], beginning with: "One should know that the self-nature of *tathatā*... and so forth.
Grasping at marks. ... [omitted] ... This concludes the third section, which provides a general enumeration of all marks and summarizes the meaning of emptiness.

As for what is called "emptiness," the phrase "from the very beginning, it is not associated with any defiled dharmas" clarifies that these defiled dharmas have, from the outset, not been associated with the intrinsically pure nature.
That is to say, "being free from the differentiated marks of all dharmas" means not only...
The defiled dharmas are entirely non-corresponding, nor do they possess any characteristic of false differentiation.

The phrase "because there is no false mental conception" demonstrates the aforementioned meaning of non-differentiation. If there were false conceptions, then characteristics of differentiation would arise;
because there is no mental conception, it is verified that there are no characteristics of differentiation.

One should know that regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), the second section below specifically dispels attachments to characteristics. This section contains two parts: first, dispelling characteristics by means of existence and non-existence;
and second, from "neither identical nor different" onwards, dispelling characteristics by means of identity and difference.
Regarding the statement that "intrinsic nature has no characteristics": all views concerning existence and non-existence arise from deluded thoughts.
Because True Suchness (Tathatā) is free from deluded thoughts, one knows that it does not possess the characteristic of existence. Someone might then say:
"If True Suchness does not have the characteristic of existence, it must then have the characteristic of non-existence. To this, I say: when I speak of it not being existent, I mean...
True Suchness (tathatā) is not existence; it is not that one desires it to be non-existence. For what reason do you say that it ought to be non-existence? Someone might say:
"If True Suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, then being neither existent nor non-existent, it should be the characteristic of True Suchness as 'neither non-existent nor non-non-existent'.
I reply: When I say True Suchness is not existence, I do not mean that it is non-existence. Furthermore, I say...
Tathatā is not non-existent; it does not mean that it is not non-existent. On what basis do you say that Tathatā is neither existent nor non-existent?

Someone might say: "If Tathatā is not 'not-existent' in the sense of appearing as existent, and is not 'not-non-existent' in the sense of appearing as non-existent, then it must be both existent and non-existent.
To this, I say: regarding the claim that it is neither existent nor non-existent, I maintain that it is Tathatā.
"It is not that it is non-existent; 'not' does not mean it is existent. True Suchness (tathatā) is not that it is non-existent;
'not' does not mean it is non-existent. Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, how could there be the meaning of being both existent and non-existent?"
Since this is the case for the four propositions regarding existence and non-existence, one may understand by analogy that the same applies to the four propositions regarding identity and difference.
Furthermore, the third section below, which provides a general summary of all characteristics, concludes by clarifying the meaning of emptiness.

As for the phrase "and so forth, generally speaking," it means that all four propositions contained within the remaining categories of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are likewise to be negated in this manner. Based on this...
Regarding all sentient beings who, possessing a deluded mind, engage in conceptual discrimination from moment to moment:

this demonstrates that these false thoughts arise and perish in every instant, and none of them correspond with the nature of the mind. Therefore, they are said to be "empty. This is a definitive designation based on the revealed meaning.

If one were apart from the deluded mind, there would truly be nothing that could be called empty. Apart from the deluded mind, there exists True Suchness (Tathatā) and [the virtues] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Merit cannot be called empty.
That which is called "not empty" refers to the subsequent explanation of the second meaning, "non-emptiness. This section consists of four parts.

Regarding the phrase "that which is not empty," this initial heading already reveals that the essence of the Dharma is not empty; the second part explains its meaning, and is therefore titled "Non-emptiness."

This third [section] establishes the name based on its meaning. Furthermore, regarding "there being no characteristics": the following fourth [section] clarifies the meaning of non-emptiness as being free from characteristics.

"Having already revealed the essence of dharmas, because it is empty and devoid of delusion" means that because there are no dharmas possessing deluded characteristics, it reveals that the essence of dharmas is originally and inherently empty;
this is precisely the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). "Constant, eternal, and unchanging" refers to the naturally pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).
It is unstained by future Buddhas and not impure with respect to past and present Buddhas. Regarding the fulfillment of pure dharmas:
apart from this True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is not a single dharma that possesses an intrinsic nature endowed with immeasurable merit;

nor is there even a single moment lacking anything. Therefore, it is called "not empty. This third [section] establishes the name based on its meaning; furthermore, it has no [discernible] characteristics.

Below, the fourth section clarifies the non-empty state that is free from characteristics. It means that there are no characteristics whatsoever to be grasped; it is also free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
"The realm beyond thought" indicates that all deluded minds are entirely non-corresponding.
"Only through realization is there correspondence" indicates that at the time of manifest realization, one is free from vitarka and vicāra, and there is neither subject nor object.

Next, the second section, the "Gate of the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind," is explained. This establishes the internal framework of the preceding "Establishment of Dharmas" by demonstrating that within it there exists the causal condition for the arising and ceasing of the mind, which is capable of revealing the essence, attributes, and functions of Mahāyāna itself.
Within this explanation, there are two parts: first, an extensive explanation of the aforementioned causal conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind;

furthermore, it is verified that [water] does not have waves as its nature. This metaphor indicates that what is above cannot be destroyed. Next, the third part of the analogy is explained:
"In this way, the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings" demonstrates that the nature of this mind is vast and great.

All sentient beings possess this. Although they remain within afflictions, the illumination of their nature does not change; therefore, it is called "pure. This corresponds to the preceding analogy of the great ocean:

the statement that it is "unmoved by ignorance" demonstrates that the nature of the mind does not itself undergo transmigration, but rather [transmigration occurs] because it is perfumed by ignorance.
The waves of the various consciousnesses arise just as ripples depend upon the wind. This defiled dharma of ignorance cannot bring about its own arising and ceasing;

rather, it arises and ceases by depending upon fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*), just as the wind depends upon water to produce movement through their conjunction. It is because of the wind that the water is stirred into waves.

Regarding the statement that "the mind and ignorance are both without form or characteristics": it means that ignorance and the mind each lack their own intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*). Regarding "they are not mutually separated":

fundamental awakening takes consciousness as its characteristic, while ignorance takes arising and ceasing as its characteristic; there is no sense of separation between this arising and ceasing and the mind.
This is like the inseparability of the nature of wind and the appearance of water mentioned above; yet, the mind is not of a moving nature—this is shown.
This pure mind does not take arising and ceasing as its nature; when combined with the water above, the water itself does not possess the nature of movement.

If it were the case that the continuity of ignorance ceases when it is extinguished, this would prove that ignorance takes arising and ceasing as its essence—just as when the wind above stops, the movement ceases.

However, the fact that the nature of wisdom remains unimpaired further demonstrates that ignorance does not take the mind as its nature. Because it does not take the mind as its nature, [ignorance is not subject to extinction].
Arising and ceasing are naturally exhausted, while the nature of wisdom remains eternally. This corresponds to the aforementioned "the moist nature is indestructible.
Next, the characteristics of inconceivable activity are explained; this section contains two parts. First, the basis upon which the activity relies is clarified.

Then, from "capable of performing all... onwards, the characteristics of the activity itself are correctly distinguished. The phrase "by relying on the purity of wisdom" clarifies the basis upon which the activity relies, namely, the *dharmakāya*.
Taking pure wisdom as the basis, the characteristics of its activity are next explained. This section further consists of two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific.

Regarding the phrase "capable of creating all supreme and wondrous objects," this clarifies the general statement; it means that based on the aforementioned pure wisdom, the response and transformation bodies, as well as the pure lands, arise to serve as the objects of perception and hearing for all sentient beings. As stated in a verse from the *Ratnagotravibhāga*:
The bodies of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are like space, without marks; for the sake of those of supreme wisdom, they act as the objects of the six sense faculties:

they manifest subtle and wondrous forms, produce the sound of Brahma-voices, cause one to smell the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts, grant the flavor of the Buddha’s sublime Dharma, and enable one to perceive the touch of samādhi.

To cause [beings] to know the profound and wondrous characteristics of the Dharma—namely, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of activity below—there are three parts within the text. "The characteristics of immeasurable merit" is the first, clarifying the excellence of activity.
"Constantly uninterrupted" and so forth is the second, clarifying the inexhaustibility of activity, which accords with the faculties of sentient beings.
The third section below correctly elucidates the functional activity [of the Buddha]. It demonstrates that this Buddha-body and its pure land are both accomplished through immeasurable merits;
therefore, they receive their preeminent names. Regarding the phrase "constantly without interruption," this second point clarifies that the activity is inexhaustible.
It is shown that, based on infinite great compassion, the two bodies arise and continue without interruption until the end of the future.

Following the capacities of sentient beings, this third section correctly explains their functional activity. There are two types of capacities among sentient beings: first, the Mahāyāna; [the second being the Hīnayāna].

Regarding the two vehicles of the Hīnayāna: Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those of the two vehicles perceive the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) with their physical eyes and thereby obtain benefit.
Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) rely upon the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), internally performing meditations such as on the pure land, and thereby obtain benefit.

Because the Tathāgata’s great compassion accords with these capacities and responses, it is called "conforming to the world. As for "spontaneous correspondence," this completes the preceding [explanation].
It is in the sense of being uninterrupted. If there were mental application (*manasikāra*), there would be interruption;

however, this great compassion is shown to arise spontaneously and constantly without the exertion of effort, and is therefore uninterrupted. Regarding "seeing various [beings] and obtaining benefit," this establishes the aforementioned meaning of following the capacities of sentient beings' faculties.
Although the natures of the faculties of sentient beings differ, the Tathāgata is able to manifest accordingly for each of them.

Manifestation. There are no [beings] who do not perceive it, for it appears in various ways according to their respective capacities and karmic conditions; thus, each gains benefit based upon their own mind.

Next, the third major section explains the meaning of the characteristics of the essence of awakening (*bodhi*) by means of analogies. This passage consists of two parts; first, the general [introduction].

The dharmas are restated and their number enumerated; they are briefly illustrated by way of analogy. As for the question "What are the four?"—this follows with the listing of names and their individual explanations.

Furthermore, regarding the essence and characteristics of awakening (*bodhi*): this reiterates the aforementioned dharmas. "There are four kinds of great meanings" is the general enumeration of the number.
"Equal to empty space" clarifies the analogy for the great meaning. "Like a pure mirror" is an analogy for the purity of the nature of mind (*cittaprakṛti*), which is capable of illumination.
This is the application; this has been briefly illustrated by way of analogy.
What are the four? Below, their names are listed individually and their meanings explained, analyzed according to the sequence of the four names.

First, the "mirror of emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā-ādarśa*) refers to being devoid of all substantial entities and the qualities of non-manifesting things. It is utterly remote from...

Regarding "the characteristics of all mental objects": this demonstrates that although this fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is inherently pure by nature, it is fundamentally incompatible with the objects of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
It is like a clear mirror: although its nature is pure, it cannot manifest the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise.
Regarding "there is no dharma that can be manifested": this is because this intrinsically pure fundamental awakening...

Regarding the manifestation of the mind's objects: since the self, sensory objects, and so forth have been non-existent from the very beginning, and because they have been non-existent from the beginning, they are not manifested by the pure mind.
This is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, which are not manifested in a clear mirror. This is not the sense of "awakened illumination."
This original enlightenment possesses no merit of cognitive illumination regarding the two kinds of objective phenomena (*viṣaya-nimitta*).

It is like a mirror that has no power of reflection toward things such as a rabbit’s horns. As for the "mirror of perfuming," this cannot act as the internal cause for the perfuming of sentient beings.
The mirror, because it possesses its own substantial nature (*svabhāva*), is able to manifest all conditioned objects; this is called "as-it-is non-emptiness" (*tathatā-aśūnyatā*).
"This mind" refers to the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which is truly not empty.
"All worldly objects" refers to all objects within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) that appear therein; this indicates that these objects have no separate basis of support.
All things manifest within the intrinsically pure fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*), just as various objects and images arise in dependence upon a mirror.
That they all appear within the mirror without ever departing from it means that when these objective realms manifested by one's own mind cease, they do not depart from outside the mind;

this is like how images in a mirror, when they vanish, do not go outside the mirror. That they do not enter [the mirror] means that even when they subsequently reappear, they do not come from the outside. Therefore...
It is said that it does not enter. Just as when a reflection appears in a mirror, it does not enter from the outside. Regarding "not lost":

when this reflection appears, because it does not enter from the outside, one cannot say it has gained entry; and when it ceases, it likewise does not go out to the outside—how then can it be called lost?
Just as when a mirror-image ceases, it cannot be called lost. Regarding "not destroyed": this refers to the reflection of the mind.
At the time of cessation, there is no intrinsic nature that can be designated as "destruction. It is like when a reflected image ceases; one cannot say that the face or the image has been destroyed.
