this refers to the six consciousnesses arising and ceasing moment by moment, whereby the perfuming of objects increases, enabling one to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings. This is because these six consciousnesses create karma based on delusion, thereby causing—
Ordinary beings undergo the suffering of segmented existence (*paricchinna-duḥkha*).
Next, regarding the third [point], the permeation by ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), the text also consists of two parts. First, the title and chapter heading state the number;
from "What are the two? onwards, the names are established and explained. First, as for "fundamental permeation" (*mūla-vāsanā*): this ignorance is of two kinds. The first...
Regarding the cause and the two fruits: this cause, which is ignorance (*avidyā*), is called the "root" because it is the basis upon which the fruits depend.

As for the phrase "because it can accomplish the meaning of karma-consciousness": since this ignorance arises constantly and without ceasing, it is able to cause the power of grasping to be accomplished.

Second, regarding the "perfuming of the views and cravings that arise": "views" refers to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); "cravings" refers to self-love (*ātma-sneha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and so forth.
These three delusions constitute ignorance at the stage of the fruit; because they arise from causes, they are termed "arising.

As for the phrase "because they can accomplish the meaning of the discerning consciousness of phenomena (*vikalpa-vijñāna*)," it means that these views and cravings differentiate between self and other, thereby establishing the capacity [of the discerning consciousness].
...the locus. Consequently, this causes the six consciousnesses to increase and blaze forth.

Regarding the fourth point, "the perfuming of True Suchness extinguishes ignorance," there are two parts within the text. First, the question: "How does perfuming give rise to pure dharmas without interruption?
This restates the preceding chapter as a query. Second, the explanation of this passage, which is further divided into two. First: [text continues]
The general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding "the two types of perfuming by the deluded mind" and below, this second section clarifies the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
From "how does perfuming give rise to pure dharmas without interruption" up to "accomplishing spontaneous activity," this clarifies the general characteristics.
Within this, the statement that "because the *tathatā* dharma exists, it is able to perfume ignorance" refers to this *tathatā*.
Previously, before one had acquired the perfuming of hearing [the Dharma], one was constantly perfumed by the defiled dharmas of ignorance.

Once one has acquired the perfuming of extensive learning and so forth, its power is increased, whereby it can then perfume ignorance. This is due to the power of the causes and conditions of such perfuming.

This essence of *tathatā* takes perfuming as its cause and functional perfuming as its condition. Because these causes and conditions are complete, there is the power of perfuming upon ignorance (*avidyā*).
This causes the deluded mind to loathe the suffering and pleasure of birth and death and to seek *nirvāṇa*.
Because this ignorance is perfumed by *tathatā*, its power is diminished. Because its power is diminished, it can further enable [the mind] to rely on...
When the deluded mind arising from ignorance comes to loathe the suffering of birth and death and joyfully seeks nirvana— because this deluded mind possesses the conditions of aversion and seeking—
it is a deluded mind that clings to objective realms when this ignorance has not yet been permeated by True Suchness (tathatā).
Once it has been perfumed, within the conditions of objective realms, it is able to give rise to the mind of aversion and seeking; this is that which perfumes the *tathatā*.
Through the power of repeatedly practicing this mind of aversion and seeking, it subsequently perfumes the *tathatā*, further augmenting its potency.

Regarding the phrase "having confidence in one's own nature, knowing that the mind is falsely moving and that there are no external objects": prior to being perfumed, one was not self-awakened to this, and [the objects] appeared [as real].

Once the false objects have been further perfumed, their power gradually increases. Because this power increases, one attains definitive and correct faith and enters the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
As for those who practice the dharma of detachment, they employ the skillful means of investigation to cultivate the contemplation of the absence of objects;

that is, by knowing as it truly is that no external objects exist. Furthermore, through the contemplation of suchness-knowledge (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), they penetrate the non-existence of external objects.
This refers to the characteristic of nature (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the aspect of contemplation at the stage of understanding (*adhimukti-avasthā*).

As for the practitioner who gives rise to various skillful means (*upāya*) in accordance with [the truth], this is the contemplation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). By conforming to *tathatā*, one gives rise to the practices of the various *pāramitās*; this is the aspect of cultivation at the stage of practice (*caryā-avasthā*).
"Neither grasping nor recollecting" means that because one knows the dependent nature manifests as if it were an object (*viṣaya*), it is not a locus of grasping; thus, it is not a locus of grasping.
Therefore, one does not grasp it. Furthermore, because one knows that what appears is like consciousness, it is not the object of recollection; therefore, one does not recollect it.

Because of this non-grasping and non-recollection, one enters the nature of non-arising within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the realization and vision of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

this is called "vision-penetration" (*darśana-prativedha*). This is the stage of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhūmi*). As for the phrase "due to long-term perfuming," it refers to the cultivation during the latter two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Regarding the statement, "By practicing the various activities, the power of the perfuming of True Suchness becomes fully satisfied, and ignorance is extinguished":
because the power of True Suchness has become fully satisfied, it is able to perfume the very last moment of ignorance until it is exhausted.
Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise; for originally, due to non-awakening, the deluded mind arises. Since ignorance is extinguished, the deluded mind [ceases].
There is no cause; logically, there is no arising. As for the statement that because there is no arising, the objective realm perishes accordingly:
this objective realm is manifested by the deluded mind. Since the deluded mind has ceased, that which was obtained through it as its cause also ceases.
Regarding the phrase "both cause and condition perish": ignorance is the cause and the deluded realm is the condition; at this point, both this cause and condition are completely exhausted. Mind...
When all characteristics are exhausted, these characteristics of the mind’s arising and ceasing are likewise exhausted along with them.
At that time, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) attains the body of liberation; this is called "attaining nirvāṇa.

Because the production of all dharmas and their functional merits within this ālayavijñāna has ceased, its basis is transformed and designated as "nirvāṇa," which is also called the "Dharmakāya. It accomplishes spontaneous activity (anābhoga-karman).
This is because, by relying on the dharma-body, it gives rise to the response and transformation bodies, performing the work of benefiting beings without effort.
Next, the explanation of the specific characteristics has two types: first, the characteristic of the deluded mind; second, the characteristic of true suchness.
"Regarding the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind, there are two kinds... up to 'swiftly proceeding toward nirvana. This clarifies the characteristics of the deluded mind.
Within this context, "deluded mind" refers to that which is produced by the ignorance that serves as the object of perfuming.

Although this deluded mind possesses the functional capacity for aversion and seeking, it is called "deluded" because its essential nature is non-awakening (*abodha*). Regarding "the meaning of perfuming has two kinds," this refers to the deluded mind.
Since there are two [types of consciousness], the perfuming of merit is likewise twofold. What are these two? This questions their two characteristics.

First, regarding the perfuming of the *vijñapti-mātra-vibhāga-śas* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena): this identifies the substance of that consciousness, while the following explains its characteristics.

"Depending on ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and so forth" clarifies the persons who give rise to this perfuming. "Those who loathe the suffering of birth and death"—this refers to how that consciousness...
The mind of birth and death possesses the capacity for weariness with suffering. "According to what one's power permits" means that one practices according to one's respective capacity.
"Gradually advancing toward the Unsurpassed Way" indicates the direction of one's progress; it shows that this is not achieved instantaneously, which is why it is said to be gradual.
Second, regarding the mental permeation (*manas-vāsanā*): next, the characteristics of the second mind are explained. Herein, "mind" refers to the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), which is constant...
It is called "mind" (*manas*) because it serves as the basis for defiled phenomena. This clarifies the arising of the consciousness that is perfumed (*vāsanā*).
The phrase "those who are bodhisattvas" clarifies the person who gives rise to this perfuming.

When this ignorance has not yet been perfumed, the mind (*manas*) that arises therefrom constantly gives rise to the four afflictions, defiling the mental consciousness and causing ordinary beings to give rise to four kinds of active (*paryavasthāna*) inversions, calculating [them] as "self" and "mine."

Furthermore, once it has been perfumed, what functional capacity does the resulting mind have toward the bodhisattvas? For one who has generated the resolve with such vigor as to swiftly proceed toward nirvāṇa,

this ādāna-vijñāna demonstrates that although it cannot defile the manovijñāna by giving rise to the notions of "I" and "mine," it can nevertheless cause the manovijñāna to think, "I am practicing non-self," and to speak in such a manner.
I alone am without equal. If this consciousness did not exist, such mental attention (*manasikāra*) could not occur either.

Next, the specific characteristics of *tathatā* (true thusness) are explained; this section consists of two parts. First is the formal explanation of perfuming (*vāsanā*), which comprises both its essence and its function.

The "Distinction" has two parts, the latter of which explains [the subject] in terms of persons. The preceding text has three sections. First, there are two types of True Suchness (tathatā) perfuming;

first, the enumeration of their number. Second, the listing of their names, beginning with "How... and so forth. Third, the explanation of their meaning, beginning with "The nature of the essence" and so forth.

The explanation of the text has two parts: first, the explanation of the essence; second, the explanation of the function, beginning with "Perfuming" and so forth, up to "The nature of the essence perfuming... and so on.

Regarding "the practitioner who has resolved their mind," this clarifies the essential nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This passage consists of two parts: first, the direct explanation of the essential nature and characteristics; second, from the question "Why?
onwards, the establishment of objections and the resolution of doubts.
Regarding "the self-substance and its characteristics mutually perfuming": this refers to the fact that the self-substance of True Suchness possesses inconceivable perfuming.
"From beginningless time" indicates that this nature of Suchness has no point of origin. "Possessing untainted dharmas" means it possesses the functional capacity to give rise to all pure dharmas.
"Being fully endowed with inconceivable activities" means that these untainted dharmas do not merely exist [statically].
Thus it is. Furthermore, there is an inconceivable activity that serves as the nature of the objective sphere for all sentient beings.
This path of True Suchness (tathatā) constitutes the essence of all phenomena and acts as the nature of the objective spheres of seeing, hearing, and so forth.

When sentient beings give rise to the consciousnesses of seeing, hearing, and so on, they are all permeated by True Suchness. Moreover, even when one dreams of following into hell or beholding rākṣasas, [it is likewise].

The arousal of the mind through weariness with suffering, or the arousal of the mind through encountering superior conditions—such as meeting assemblies of ordinary or holy beings—and hearing the teachings on defiled phenomena, all arise from the power of internal permeation by True Suchness (*tathatā*).

These two meanings refer to the two aspects of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and inconceivable karma. As for "constant permeation," these two meanings do not exist prior to the process of permeation itself.

It begins, yet it has no end. Regarding "because it possesses power": prior to obtaining the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*), there is only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but not yet the capacity for wearying detachment (*nirveda*).
Only after hearing the permeation of the Dharma does one subsequently possess this power.
That which can cause sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth and death, and even to resolve to practice, demonstrates the power of permeation.

Next, the refutation is established to resolve doubts. First is the question; second is the answer. This refutation consists of four parts: first, "If it were thus," which restates the core tenet of the preceding argument;
second, "All sentient beings," which establishes a hypothetical concession; third, "How could... and so forth, which sets forth two simultaneous difficulties.

All should simultaneously descend [to the fourth point] to resolve the objection. Within this, if the meaning is as follows, it describes the Master’s established doctrine that True Suchness permeates sentient beings:
that all sentient beings possess True Suchness and so forth, and are all thus permeated by cultivation.
This is the second point establishing the meaning of permeation (*vāsanā*): that all sentient beings, whether ordinary or noble, are permeated by True Suchness (*tathatā*).

As for the question of why some have faith while others do not—this constitutes the third section, which sets forth the dual difficulties regarding faith and lack of faith, as well as the two difficulties concerning priority and posteriority.
If it is the case that the arising of faith in sentient beings occurs only because they are permeated by True Suchness, then this True Suchness...
The nature [of suchness] exists equally in all sentient beings, and the meaning of being perfumed is likewise uniform. If this were so, then faith should arise simultaneously for all.
Why is it that some possess faith while others lack it, with immeasurable distinctions of before and after? This True Suchness (tathatā) has no limits of beginning or end.
If those sentient beings who can be perfumed were to attain faith, they should produce that faith at one and the same time. How then could there be a sequential arising of faith?

There are immeasurable distinctions. If such a principle were actually existent, there would be no sequence of before and after; everything should occur simultaneously. This concludes the fourth section on resolving the objection.
Next, the response to this is threefold: first, because of differences in thickness [of spiritual capacity], there is belief or lack of belief; second, the arising of afflictions...
Because there is a sequence of before and after, there is prior faith and subsequent faith. Because the three causal conditions are either complete or incomplete, there is faith and non-faith.

Within this, that which is real is fundamentally one, yet possesses immeasurable and boundless ignorance. This means that within this *tathatā* (suchness), there exists the principle of non-awakening (*abodha*) equal in number to the sands of the Ganges.
That these are "differentiated by their intrinsic nature from the very beginning" refers to this principle of non-awakening.
The functional capacity of *tathatā* (suchness) is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because its density varies, sentient beings arise through the principle of non-awakening (*abodha*).
These illusory sentient beings do not recognize their own illusoriness; therefore, they give rise to the notions of "self" and "mine," which manifest in varying degrees of lightness and heaviness.
It perfumes ignorance, whereby it subsequently becomes either thick or thin. That which is thin possesses faith; that which is thick lacks faith.
It is for this reason that such differences exist.
